title: Do Analogies Work? How Do We Know?
author: Lee LeFever
summary: Lee LeFever uses a classic 1980s study by Mary Gick and Keith Holyoak to test whether analogies really help people transfer understanding from one situation to another. Participants read two stories about dividing forces and converging on a target, one about a general and a fortress and one about firefighters and hoses, and were then asked what the stories had in common. They were sorted into good, intermediate and poor groups by how clearly they saw the convergence pattern, and then asked to solve a tumor radiation problem that has the same structure. Ninety-one percent of the good group solved it, against forty percent of the intermediate group and thirty percent of the poor group. LeFever concludes that explainers should not assume others see the connection they see, and that making the pattern explicit and showing it in other settings makes knowledge more transferable. The post also opens with a short note on why he writes the newsletter.
points: Gick and Holyoak's experiment tests whether learning relationships in one situation helps people solve a structurally similar problem in a different one.
Not everyone notices the same patterns, since some participants saw convergence while others saw only teamwork or military exercises.
Seeing the pattern strongly predicted success, with 91 percent of the good group solving the radiation problem against 30 percent of the poor group.
Explainers should walk through the pattern and show which relationships matter instead of assuming the audience sees the connection.
Naming the pattern and then demonstrating it in other situations makes the knowledge more likely to be applied and remembered later.
quotes: A well-placed analogy can feel like a shortcut. Once we understand one phenomenon, we can start to see connections to others.
Mary Gick and Keith Holyoak conducted fascinating experiments to help answer this question.
The takeaway: Not everyone sees the same kinds of connections. Some people see patterns; others just see teamwork or military exercises.
The results were stark. People who saw the convergence pattern were much more likely to use it in a different situation.
Of the participants in the “good” category, 91% solved the radiation problem (10 of 11 people)
First, when we see a connection, it’s easy to assume that everyone else sees it too. They don’t. Instead of assuming, make the important connections clear.
Second, this kind of knowledge is transferable. Once the audience sees and can describe the pattern, they are more likely to apply it later.
